reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant migraine with aura defined by fully reversible motor weakness (hemiparesis) during the aura phase
Three principal genes are recognised: CACNA1A (a P/Q-type calcium-channel subunit, FHM1), ATP1A2 (a sodium-potassium ATPase subunit, FHM2) and SCN1A (a neuronal sodium channel, FHM3)
The aura typically evolves over minutes and includes motor weakness alongside visual, sensory and dysphasic symptoms, followed by headache
Attacks can be severe, with prolonged hemiparesis, confusion, fever, seizures and even coma in some CACNA1A-related cases
FHM1 (CACNA1A) may be associated with progressive cerebellar ataxia and nystagmus between attacks
The underlying mechanism is thought to be a lowered threshold for cortical spreading depression driven by disturbed ion transport and glutamate handling
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by family history and genetic testing, after excluding stroke and structural or vascular causes
reference.pathophysiology: Familial hemiplegic migraine is caused by autosomal dominant variants in genes controlling neuronal ion homeostasis: CACNA1A (P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel), ATP1A2 (the astrocytic sodium-potassium ATPase) and SCN1A (a neuronal sodium channel). These variants increase synaptic glutamate availability and neuronal excitability, or impair clearance of potassium and glutamate, lowering the threshold for cortical spreading depression, the slow wave of neuronal and glial depolarisation that underlies migraine aura. The motor weakness reflects spread of this depolarising wave across motor cortex, and the shared final pathway explains why distinct channel and pump defects produce a similar clinical syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack
CADASIL and other hereditary small-vessel diseases
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI with vascular imaging to exclude stroke and structural lesions
Genetic testing of CACNA1A, ATP1A2 and SCN1A
Electroencephalography during or after prolonged attacks to exclude seizures
Detailed family history and pedigree analysis
Cerebrospinal fluid examination in atypical or first severe attacks to exclude alternative causes
Metabolic and mitochondrial workup where the phenotype is atypical
redFlags: First-ever episode of hemiparesis, where acute stroke must be excluded urgently
Prolonged coma, fever or seizures during an attack
Progressive interictal cerebellar signs suggesting a wider CACNA1A phenotype
Persistent focal deficit after the expected recovery period
reference.prognosis: Between attacks most patients are neurologically well, and individual episodes, although alarming, are usually fully reversible. Attack frequency and severity vary widely; some CACNA1A-associated cases carry a risk of severe prolonged attacks or progressive cerebellar ataxia, so the outlook depends on the specific genotype and phenotype.
pitfalls: Failing to exclude acute stroke at the first presentation of hemiparesis
Prescribing vasoconstrictive acute migraine therapies that are generally avoided in hemiplegic migraine
Attributing prolonged confusion or coma solely to encephalitis or stroke and missing a severe FHM attack
Overlooking interictal cerebellar signs that point to a CACNA1A cause
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Acute attack treatment with simple analgesics such as NSAIDs or paracetamol and antiemetics, traditionally avoiding vasoconstrictor triptans and ergots given the prominent aura
Preventive therapy for frequent or disabling attacks with agents such as verapamil, acetazolamide, lamotrigine or topiramate
Identification and avoidance of triggers, including minor head trauma and cerebral angiography, which can provoke severe attacks
Supportive management of prolonged severe attacks with confusion, fever or seizures, including monitoring and seizure control where needed
Brain imaging to exclude stroke in the acute setting given the focal neurological deficit
Genetic counselling with CACNA1A, ATP1A2 and SCN1A testing and family evaluation
Neurology referral, with surveillance for progressive cerebellar ataxia in CACNA1A-related disease
